Q: When would the -e, --editable option be useful with pip install? A:

Concrete example of using --editable in development

If you play with this test package as in:

cd ~
git clone https://github.com/cirosantilli/vcdvcd
cd vcdvcd
# git checkout 515273543d74da21588785a2b192159c8ac7a66a
virtualenv -p python3 .venv
virtualenv -p python3 .venv
pip install --editable .

it outputs:

Obtaining file:///home/ciro/bak/git/vcdvcd
  Installing build dependencies ... done
  Checking if build backend supports build_editable ... done
  Getting requirements to build editable ... done
  Preparing editable metadata (pyproject.toml) ... done
Building wheels for collected packages: vcdvcd
  Building editable for vcdvcd (pyproject.toml) ... done
  Created wheel for vcdvcd: filename=vcdvcd-2.6.0-0.editable-py3-none-any.whl size=8112 sha256=ab4f0a99d4e973777d70057939bc0a328edd86599bff65df71639e54a4980916
  Stored in directory: /tmp/pip-ephem-wheel-cache-67bw6xr4/wheels/be/77/05/49efafc246f927e33eae4d67091f78cbe926d8f368804f717a
Successfully built vcdvcd
Installing collected packages: vcdvcd
Successfully installed vcdvcd-2.6.0

Before Ubuntu 23.04, you didn't need to use the virtual environment, but 23.04 started forbidding people from breaking their systems by installing packages globally with pip with the externally-managed-environment thingy, which is probably a good thing, and using a virtual environment became mandatory.

From now on, so long as you are inside the virtualenv, importeres of vcdvcd will pick up the current library as it is without the need for a further pip install:

python -c 'import vcdvcd'

You can test that for example by adding some gibberish to the library file, e.g. add an asdf to it:

diff --git a/vcdvcd/vcdvcd.py b/vcdvcd/vcdvcd.py
index 5b31f12..d2f9b66 100644
--- a/vcdvcd/vcdvcd.py
+++ b/vcdvcd/vcdvcd.py
@@ -1,5 +1,5 @@
 from __future__ import print_function
-
+asdf
 import bisect
 import io
 import math

and then watch it blow up on the next invocation:

$ python -c 'import vcdvcd'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<string>", line 1, in <module>
    import vcdvcd
  File "/home/ciro/bak/git/vcdvcd/vcdvcd/__init__.py", line 1, in <module>
    from .vcdvcd import *
  File "/home/ciro/bak/git/vcdvcd/vcdvcd/vcdvcd.py", line 2, in <module>
    asdf
NameError: name 'asdf' is not defined

The way this works is that -e made pip create files:

.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/__editable__.vcdvcd-2.6.0.pth
.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/__editable___vcdvcd_2_6_0_finder.py

which together act as a "symlink" to the Python interpreter and make it correctly search for the library at that Git repo's path.

Note however that executable files installed with --editable, such as the vcdcat script provided by that package via scripts= on setup.py, do not get symlinked, just copied directly to:

.venv/bin/vcdcat

just like for regular installs, and therefore updates to the git repository won't directly affect them automatically which is a shame. The workarounds are, from inside the virtual environment:

  • call the executable directly, e.g. bin/vcdcat
  • add it to the front of the PATH after you start the virtual environment: export PATH="$PWD/bin:$PATH"

By comparison, a regular non --editable install from the git source:

pip uninstall vcdvcd
pip install .

produces a copy of the installed files under:

.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/vcdvcd

and so things don't get automatically updated.

Uninstall of an editable package as done above requires a new enough pip as mentioned at: How to uninstall editable packages with pip (installed with -e)

Tested in Python 3.13.7, pip 25.1.1, Ubuntu 25.10.

Recommendation: develop directly in-tree whenever possible

The editable setup is useful when you are testing your patch to a package through another project.

If however you can fully test your change in-tree, just do that instead of generating an editable install which is more complex.

E.g., the vcdvcd package above is setup in a way that you can just cd into the source and do ./vcdcat without pip installing the package itself (in general, you might need to install dependencies from requirements.txt though), and the import vcdvcd that that executable does (or possibly your own custom test) just finds the package correctly in the same directory it lives in.

pipx install -e

pipx is the thing that was introduced to overcome externally-managed-environment to allow people to easily install executables globally without the need for manually activating a virtualenv each time.

pipx install also has an -e option which has a similar effect to pip install -e, e.g. you can do:

cd vcdvcd
pipx install -e .

and how, vcdcat is installed globally and updates to the library will automatically reflect on it.

Much like pip install -e however, updates to vcdcat itself won't be reflected.

Original Answer:

I didn't want to restart Chrome and disable my web security (because I was browsing while developing) and stumbled onto this Chrome extension.

Chrome Web Store Allow-Control-Allow-Origin: *
(https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/allow-control-allow-origi/nlfbmbojpeacfghkpbjhddihlkkiljbi?hl=en)

Basically it's a little toggle switch to toggle on and off the Allow-Access-Origin-Control check. Works perfectly for me for what I'm doing.

Q: Bicubic, Bilinear, and Nearest-Neighbor Resampling for Image Resizing A:

The key issue is not the exact coordinate convention. There are several valid ones: align corners, half-pixel offsets, pixel-area alignment, etc. As already explained previously, the important point is the mapping direction: ordinary resize/resample is normally done with backward mapping, not naive forward mapping. A naive source-to-destination loop is incomplete unless it is turned into splatting, accumulation, or footprint rasterization.

This is not about GPU computation or efficient GPU implementation. The point is simply that some methods commonly associated with texture mapping or GPU rendering, such as trilinear or anisotropic filtering, are ALSO resampling methods worth mentioning. They can be implemented on CPU as well, although a good CPU implementation, especially for anisotropic or footprint-based resampling, is not necessarily trivial or cheap.

So image resizing should not be presented as a choice between four or five named "standard" interpolation modes. The real design choices are backward vs forward mapping, upsampling vs downsampling, point sampling vs area/footprint filtering, filter quality vs ringing/blur, and the computation budget available.
